content: Dr. Bernard J. Cigrand, a dentist by profession, is widely regarded as the father of Flag Day in the United States. Born in 1866 and passing in 1932, he practiced dentistry in Chicago and served as the third dean of the University of Illinois at Chicago College of Dentistry from 1903 to 1906. His contributions to the establishment of Flag Day began in 1885 when, as a grade school teacher in Waubeka, Wisconsin, he organized the first formal observance of Flag Day at Stony Hill School. This school has since been restored, and a bust of Dr. Cigrand is displayed at the National Flag Day Americanism Center in Waubeka to honor his legacy. From the late 1880s onward, Dr. Cigrand traveled extensively across the United States, delivering speeches that emphasized patriotism, respect for the American flag, and the importance of an annual Flag Day observance on June 14. This date marks the anniversary of the Continental Congress's adoption of the Stars and Stripes in 1777. He became the president of the American Flag Day Association and later the National Flag Day Society, which provided him with organizational support to further his cause. Dr. Cigrand once stated that he had delivered 2,188 speeches on the topics of patriotism and the flag. In 1899, Dr. Cigrand joined the teaching staff at the University of Illinois at Chicago College of Dentistry. The following year, in 1900, he was elected by the faculty to represent the institution at the Paris International Congress of Educators. He also served as the secretary of the faculty before being appointed dean. After his tenure as dean, he continued to teach at the college well into the 1920s. Additionally, he was a prolific writer, contributing articles to five Chicago newspapers. Dr. Cigrand's tireless advocacy for Flag Day culminated in 1916 when, after 30 years of his efforts, President Woodrow Wilson officially proclaimed June 14 as Flag Day. This proclamation was later codified into law by the United States Congress in 1949. The public widely credited Dr. Cigrand as the Father of Flag Day, with the Chicago Tribune remarking that he almost singlehandedly established the holiday.
